h1: Arizona Disability Property Tax Exemption Appeal Letter Generator
metaTitle: Arizona Disability Tax Exemption Appeal Demand Letter
metaDescription: Generate an Arizona disability property tax exemption appeal demand letter. State-specific guidance on deadlines, statutes, and assessor disputes.
deadline: Sixty days after the notice of valuation is mailed, to petition the assessor (A.R.S. § 42-16051)
penalty: Reinstatement of the exemption and a corrected tax bill
introParagraph: If you are a person with a total and permanent disability in Arizona and your county assessor denied or removed your property tax exemption, you have a limited window to fight back. Assessors reject applications for missing paperwork, outdated certifications, or calculation errors, and a well-drafted appeal letter that cites the correct Arizona statutes, attaches the required proof, and meets the deadline can resolve the dispute without going to court. This page explains the appeal path and what your letter should contain.
lawExplanation: A.R.S. § 42-11111 provides exemptions for widows and widowers, persons with total and permanent disabilities, and veterans with service or nonservice connected disabilities, subject to the qualifications stated in the statute. When initially claiming an exemption, the claimant files an affidavit under penalty of perjury (A.R.S. § 42-11152). If the assessor denies the exemption or removes one previously granted, the owner may petition the assessor on the prescribed form within sixty days after the notice of valuation is mailed (A.R.S. § 42-16051). If the assessor denies relief, A.R.S. § 42-16056 allows an appeal within twenty-five days after the decision is mailed, to the county board of equalization (or the state board where no county board exists) or to superior court. An owner may also appeal to court under A.R.S. § 42-16201, directly on or before December 15 or within sixty days after the most recent administrative decision on a petition. The tax court is the tax department of the superior court in Maricopa County (A.R.S. § 12-161). Check the current text of A.R.S. § 42-11111 for the qualification limits that apply to you.
letterStrategy: Address the letter to the county assessor who issued the denial. Open by identifying the parcel number, tax year, and the notice you are appealing. Cite A.R.S. § 42-11111 and state the qualification you meet, and attach the supporting documents the assessor requested. If the denial cited a missing document, address that first. Set a reasonable response date and state that you will petition under A.R.S. § 42-16051 and pursue further appeal if the exemption is not reinstated. Request a corrected tax bill and a refund or credit for any excess taxes paid. Send by certified mail with return receipt and keep a complete copy to prove timely filing.
proceduralNotes: The tax court is the tax department of the superior court in Maricopa County (A.R.S. § 12-161). A taxpayer may elect small claims procedures under A.R.S. § 12-172 for class three property or where the full cash value is two million dollars or less (valuation disputes). Key dates: sixty days after the notice of valuation is mailed to petition the assessor (A.R.S. § 42-16051), and December 15 for a direct court appeal under A.R.S. § 42-16201. Confirm all dates against your own notice.

faq.q: Who qualifies for Arizona's disability property tax exemption?
faq.a: A.R.S. § 42-11111 provides an exemption for persons with total and permanent disabilities, subject to the qualifications in the statute. Read the current text of the statute or ask your county assessor for the application and the limits that apply to you.

faq.q: How do I claim the exemption?
faq.a: When initially claiming an exemption, you file an affidavit under penalty of perjury with the assessor (A.R.S. § 42-11152). Ask the assessor's office which supporting documents it requires.

faq.q: What is the deadline to appeal a denial?
faq.a: You may petition the assessor within sixty days after the notice of valuation is mailed (A.R.S. § 42-16051). If the assessor denies relief, you have twenty-five days after the decision is mailed to appeal to the board of equalization or superior court (A.R.S. § 42-16056). A direct court appeal is available under A.R.S. § 42-16201 on or before December 15.

faq.q: What if the assessor denies my appeal?
faq.a: You can appeal to the county board of equalization (or the state board where no county board exists) or to superior court within twenty-five days after the decision is mailed (A.R.S. § 42-16056), and then to court under A.R.S. § 42-16201.
No. Property owners can send the letter and file the petition themselves. If your case proceeds to the board or the tax court, a property tax attorney or licensed tax agent can help.
